problem: "constantly discernible" became "everywhere" (different claim); "manners" (moeurs) not rendered as customs per STYLE-NOTE.
replacement: The settlers of New England were at once ardent sectarians and daring innovators. Some of their religious opinions were very narrow, but they were entirely free of political prejudices. Two tendencies followed from this. They were distinct but not opposed, and they can be constantly seen in the customs as well as in the laws of the country.

problem: "adapted" replaced by "settled" and "agitated" by "unsettled", losing the antithesis and the source words.
replacement: Political principles and all human laws and institutions were shaped and changed at their pleasure. The barriers of the society they were born in fell before them, and the old principles that had governed the world for ages were gone. A path with no turning and a field with no horizon opened up to the eager, exploring curiosity of man. But at the boundary of the political world he stops his inquiries. He prudently sets aside the use of his most formidable faculties. He no longer agrees to doubt or to innovate. He carefully avoids lifting the curtain of the sanctuary, and he yields with submissive respect to truths that he will not discuss. So in the moral world everything is classified, adjusted, decided, and foreseen, while in the political world everything is stirred up, uncertain, and disputed. In the one there is a passive, though voluntary, obedience. In the other there is an independence that scorns experience and is jealous of authority.

problem: Ungrammatical run-on: "seem very different, yet far from conflicting, they advance together".
replacement: These two tendencies seem very different, yet they are far from conflicting. They advance together and support each other. Religion sees that civil liberty gives the faculties of man a noble field of exercise, and that the political world is a field the Creator prepared for the efforts of the intelligence. Religion is content with the freedom and power it enjoys in its own sphere and with the place it holds. Its empire is never more securely established than when it reigns in the hearts of men with no support beyond its own native strength. Religion is no less the companion of liberty in all its battles and triumphs, the cradle of its infancy, and the divine source of its claims. Religion is the safeguard of morality, and morality is the best security of law and the surest pledge of freedom. *m

problem: Source dashes turned into full stops and a rephrased fragment; STYLE-NOTE requires spaced em dashes (cf. 4:2).
replacement: Remains of aristocratic institutions in the midst of a complete democracy — Why? — Distinction to be carefully drawn between what is of Puritan origin and what is of English origin.

The reader is cautioned not to draw too general or too absolute a conclusion from what has been said. The social condition, the religion, and the customs of the first emigrants undoubtedly had an immense influence on the destiny of their new country. Nevertheless, they were not in a position to found a state of things that depended on them alone. No one can entirely shake off the influence of the past. The settlers, whether they meant to or not, mixed habits and ideas that came from their education and from the traditions of their country with the habits and ideas that were purely their own. To judge the Anglo-Americans of the present day, it is therefore necessary to distinguish what is of Puritan origin from what is of English origin.

problem: "manners" (moeurs) kept while "usages" became "customs"; STYLE-NOTE term rule.
replacement: A social condition is usually the result of circumstances, sometimes of laws, and more often of the two together. But wherever it exists, it can rightly be seen as the source of almost all the laws, practices, and ideas that govern the conduct of nations. Whatever it does not produce, it modifies. Anyone who wants to understand the legislation and the customs of a nation must therefore begin by studying its social condition.

problem: "have not attributed to this law a greater influence" became "given this law a greater influence" (reads as granting, not recognizing); causal "for" dropped.
replacement: But the law of descent was the last step toward equality. I am surprised that ancient and modern jurists have not recognized a greater influence of this law on human affairs. *a It is true that these laws belong to civil affairs. Nevertheless, they ought to be placed at the head of all political institutions, for political laws are only the symbol of a nation’s condition, whereas these laws exercise an incredible influence on its social state. They also operate on society in a sure and uniform way, reaching, as it were, generations not yet born.

problem: Footnote prose left verbatim in 1862 wording ("disposed to", "furnished with the means", "incites"); STYLE-NOTE requires modernizing a note's own prose.
replacement: c [ Land being the most stable kind of property, we find from time to time rich individuals who are willing to make great sacrifices to obtain it, and who gladly give up a considerable part of their income to make sure of the rest. But these are accidental cases. The preference for landed property is no longer found habitually in any class except the poor. The small landowner, who has less information, less imagination, and fewer passions than the great one, is generally occupied with the desire of increasing his estate, and it often happens that through inheritance, marriage, or the chances of trade he is gradually given the means. Thus, to balance the tendency that leads men to divide their estates, there exists another that urges them to add to them. This tendency is enough to prevent estates from being divided ad infinitum, but it is not strong enough to create great territorial possessions, and certainly not to keep them up in the same family.]

problem: "has no existence" became "does not yet exist": adds an expectation not in the source.
replacement: This picture, which may perhaps seem exaggerated, still gives a very imperfect idea of what is happening in the new States of the West and Southwest. At the end of the last century, a few bold adventurers began to push into the valleys of the Mississippi, and the mass of the population soon began to move in that direction. Communities never heard of before were seen to rise from the wilderness. States whose names had not existed a few years earlier took their place in the American Union. In the Western settlements we can see democracy at its utmost extreme. These States were founded on the spur of the moment and, so to speak, by chance, and their inhabitants are people of yesterday. They hardly know one another, and even the nearest neighbors do not know each other’s history. In this part of the American continent, therefore, the population has not felt the influence of great names and great wealth, or even that of the natural aristocracy of knowledge and virtue. No one is there to wield the respected power that men willingly give to the memory of a life spent doing good before their eyes. The new States of the West already have inhabitants, but society does not exist among them. *e
